newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Olivetti plunges as trading resumes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Olivetti plunges as trading resumes.

text.p: Shares in Italian high-tech group Olivetti plunged on the Milan stock exchange on Monday when trading resumed after a two-day suspension as investors expressed doubts that the group can survive in its present form.
Olivetti's stock opened at 619 lire, a fall of 17.4 percent from Wednesday when it had last traded at 749.4 lire before the suspension was announced.

Stock market regulator Consob had called a halt to trading when Olivetti's recently-hired director general Renzo Francesconi resigned abruptly on Wednesday after questioning the accuracy of the company's first-half results.

Francesconi's departure came one day after the resignation from the board of Carlo De Benedetti, who spent 18 years as chairman of the loss-making supplier of personal computers, office equipment and systems integration services.
A top trade union official in the northwest region of Piedmont, where Olivetti is based, fuelled the mood of crisis on Monday, saying that up to 5,000 jobs at the firm could now be at risk.

"Olivetti is in the throes of a dramatic crisis, there is talk at the highest levels in the company of thousands of sackings. We heard rumours on Saturday of 5,000 redundancies," said Giorgio Cremaschi, an official at the Fiom metalworkers' union.
Olivetti is engaged in a painful transition from data processing businesses to telecommuniocations services, seen as the money-spinner of the 1990s.

The resumption of stock dealing in Olivetti was held up for two hours on Monday morning until Consob widened fluctuation bands to 20 percent from 15 percent, thereby allowing the shares to find a new trading level.
Olivetti issued a statement on Friday evening defending its accounting practices and saying that its figures for the first six months of 1996 were in order.
Consob has said that it will continue its investigation of Olivetti's accounts and plans to meet the company's internal auditors this week.

Investors were taken aback by a worse-than-expected first half pre-tax loss of 440.8 billion lire ($291.5 million) at Olivetti, including a 200 billion provision to slim down loss-making parts of the business.
Milan brokerage house Pasfin advised its clients last week not to invest in Olivetti shares unless there was a dramatic reversal in the company's fortunes.

"We consider that the (Olivetti) stock poses such a risk that we advise against purchasing it before a serious rescue attempt is attempted," Pasfin equities analyst Alberto Rolla said in a note to clients.

An investment banker in Milan, who asked not to be named, said Olivetti could not survive without shutting down or selling off unprofitable parts of the business, in particular the ailing personal computers subsidiary.
"They have to do a lot before they have a self-sustaining entity," said the banker.

Investors were shaken to discover last week that Olivetti's traditionally lucrative activities such as office printers and fax machines were suffering an erosion in profits in the face of keen competition from U.S. and Japanese rivals. ($1=1512 Lire)
